_readme: One entry per partner. Edit here, then run `python3 partners/build.py` to regenerate partners/<slug>/index.html and partners/index.html. Empty strings and empty lists are fine: the page simply omits that section. Fields: slug (URL), name, url (their site), tagline (one line), tags (3), cohort (label shown on the page, e.g. '2026 cohort'), term (e.g. '2026–2031'), led_by, serves, offers (list of short items), what (1 paragraph, their words), why (1 paragraph, ASF's words), quote {text, who}, funding (1 paragraph), numbers (list of {value, label}), donate, contact, photo (path relative to the partner's folder, or empty).

partners.name: Black E.S.T.E.E.M.
partners.tagline: Hands-on STEM, leadership, and entrepreneurship programs building confidence and career pathways for Black girls ages 8–16 across the GTA.
partners.serves: Black girls ages 8–16 across the Greater Toronto Area
offers: Hands-on STEM workshops and camps
Leadership and mentorship programs
Entrepreneurship training for teens
Exposure to Black women in science, technology, engineering, and business
partners.what: Black E.S.T.E.E.M. (Entrepreneurs, Scientists, Technicians, Engineers, Economists, Mathematicians) runs hands-on programs where Black girls build, code, experiment, pitch, and lead. The organization started as a founder-led grassroots effort and has grown into a GTA-wide program with workshops, camps, and a network of mentors drawn from the fields the girls are being introduced to.
partners.why: Black E.S.T.E.E.M. is Black-led, grassroots, and working at the point where confidence is built or lost: ages 8 to 16. The organization has grown steadily on a small budget, which told our advisory council the model works and that unrestricted, multi-year funding would let it plan beyond the next workshop.

partners.name: MIND Program
partners.tagline: Moving In New Directions delivers free homemade meals and on-site food banks to Toronto Community Housing residents in Scarborough facing food insecurity.
partners.serves: Toronto Community Housing residents in Scarborough facing food insecurity
offers: Free homemade meals delivered to community housing sites
On-site food banks
Partnerships with frontline agencies already working in each building
partners.what: MIND Program (Moving In New Directions) brings food to where people already are. Working through frontline organizations in Toronto Community Housing buildings in Scarborough, MIND delivers free homemade meals and runs on-site food banks for residents who cannot easily get to a food bank across the city. The meals are cooked, not pre-packaged, and the program is built around the dignity of the people receiving them.
partners.why: MIND solves a logistics problem most food programs do not: it goes to the building instead of asking people to come to it. It is small, direct, and run with care, and its partnerships with frontline agencies mean every dollar reaches residents rather than overhead. Our advisory council saw an organization that would do more with steady, flexible funding than with another one-year project grant.

partners.name: Oasis Youth Care Programs
partners.tagline: Transitional housing and wrap-around support helping Black and racialized youth in Halton and Peel move from homelessness to stable, permanent homes.
partners.serves: Black and racialized youth experiencing homelessness in Halton and Peel Regions
offers: Oasis House transitional homes in Oakville
A resource centre for youth not in residence
Case management, life skills, and housing search support
A path to permanent housing, with follow-up after move-out
partners.what: Oasis Youth Care Programs runs transitional homes for young people who have nowhere stable to live, and surrounds that housing with the support it takes to leave it well: case management, life skills, help with school and work, and a housing search that ends in a lease. Oasis is based in Oakville and serves Halton and Peel, suburbs where youth homelessness is real but services are thin.
partners.why: Youth homelessness in the 905 is under-served and under-counted, and Oasis is one of the few organizations built specifically for Black and racialized youth there. It launched its transitional housing model in 2020 and has kept it running through the hardest years for the sector. Our advisory council chose Oasis because the model is clear, the leadership is close to the youth it serves, and multi-year funding lets a housing program plan in years instead of months.

partners.name: Power To Girls Foundation
partners.tagline: School-based mentorship, leadership, and wellness programming that builds sisterhood and self-worth for Black girls and young women across the GTA.
partners.serves: Black girls and young women across the Greater Toronto Area
offers: School-based mentorship circles
Leadership and wellness programming
Annual conferences and summer opportunities
The MY Power app
Youth-led research on the experiences of Black girls in Ontario schools
partners.what: Power To Girls runs mentorship and leadership programs inside schools, where Black girls spend most of their day and where, too often, they are overlooked or over-disciplined. Programs are built around sisterhood: small circles, consistent mentors, and space to be a whole person. The organization also does its own research, including a multi-year study of Black girls' educational experiences across Ontario, and uses it to shape what it offers.
partners.why: Power To Girls pairs direct programming with research the girls themselves help design, which is rare for an organization its size. It is Black-led and has built relationships with schools that took years to earn. Our advisory council chose it because the work is rooted in the community it serves and because unrestricted funding lets the organization keep its mentors and programs steady from one school year to the next.

partners.name: Sawubona Africentric Circle of Support
partners.tagline: Culturally responsive caregiver support, workshops, and advocacy for Black families raising children and adults with disabilities.
partners.led_by: Sherron Grant and Clovis Grant, Co-founders
partners.serves: Black families in the GTA raising children and adults with disabilities and special needs
offers: Peer support circles for caregivers
One-to-one help navigating services and funding
Workshops and a caregiver toolkit in English and French
Community events that bring isolated families together
Advocacy within the disability and education systems
partners.what: Sawubona is a Zulu greeting that means "I see you." The organization was founded by parents who found that disability services were not built with Black families in mind, and who wanted a place where families like theirs could be seen. It runs peer support circles, one-to-one navigation support, workshops, and community gatherings, and equips caregivers to advocate for their family members inside systems that are often hard to move.
partners.why: Sawubona works at the intersection of two communities that each face barriers on their own, and it was built by the people living that experience. It has delivered steadily for years on project funding and has a five-year plan for what comes next. Our advisory council chose Sawubona because the need is clear, the leadership is trusted by the families it serves, and multi-year funding lets a caregiver-led organization stop fundraising long enough to grow.

partners.name: Black Creek Community Farm
partners.tagline: An urban agricultural centre rooted in Toronto's Jane and Finch neighbourhood, engaging diverse communities through sustainable food.
partners.serves: Residents of Jane and Finch and surrounding northwest Toronto neighbourhoods
offers: A working farm inside the city
Fresh, affordable produce for the neighbourhood
Youth and community programming on the land
partners.what: Black Creek Community Farm is a working farm in Jane and Finch, one of Toronto's most diverse and least-served neighbourhoods. It grows food for the community, employs and trains local residents and youth, and uses the land as a gathering place for education, culture, and food justice work.
partners.why: Few organizations connect food access, youth employment, and community pride on a single site the way Black Creek does. It is rooted in its neighbourhood and led from within it, and our partnership supports work that has to be planned in growing seasons, not grant cycles.

partners.name: Community Justice Collective
partners.tagline: Legal support for community organizers and social justice movements across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area.
partners.serves: Community organizers, tenants, and social movements across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area
offers: Legal advice and representation for organizers and movements
Know-your-rights education
Support for tenant and community campaigns
partners.what: Community Justice Collective is a movement lawyering organization. It provides legal support to the organizers, tenant groups, and grassroots campaigns that larger legal clinics cannot take on, and it does so as a partner in the work rather than a service provider at arm's length.
partners.why: Movement lawyering is almost impossible to fund through conventional project grants, and CJC fills a gap no larger institution does. Our partnership supports the legal infrastructure that community organizing in the GTHA depends on.

partners.name: Homeless Connect Toronto
partners.tagline: Coordinates "one-stop-shop" events connecting people at risk of or experiencing homelessness with the supports they need.
partners.serves: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness in Toronto
offers: Large one-day service events bringing dozens of providers under one roof
Health care, ID, housing, employment, and legal supports on site
A volunteer base drawn from across the city
partners.what: Homeless Connect Toronto runs events where someone who is homeless or close to it can, in a single day, see a doctor, replace lost ID, talk to a housing worker, get a haircut, and sit down for a meal. The organization's work is bringing the system to the person, once, in one place, instead of asking them to navigate it alone.
partners.why: Homeless Connect is volunteer-driven and lean, and it solves a coordination problem the sector has struggled with for years. Our partnership supports an organization that makes the rest of the system work better for the people who need it most.

partners.name: ENAGB Indigenous Youth Agency
partners.tagline: Cultural, employment, life-skills, and wellness programs designed by and for Indigenous youth ages 12–29 in Toronto.
partners.serves: Indigenous youth ages 12–29 in Toronto, and families with children 0–6 through its EarlyON program
offers: Cultural programming and land-based learning
Employment and life-skills training
Holistic wellness and recreation
An EarlyON program for Indigenous families
An annual cultural festival and competition powwow
partners.what: ENAGB — Eshkiniigjik Naandwechigegamig, Aabiish Gaa Binjibaaying: a place for healing our youth; where did we come from? — is an Indigenous-led youth agency in Toronto. Its programs are designed through Indigenous youth participation and are built to grow self-esteem, confidence, skills, and self-determination, with culture at the centre: ceremony, land-based learning, and a Youth Council that shapes what the agency does.
partners.why: ENAGB is led by the youth it serves, through a Youth Council with real authority, and it has grown from a small program into a city-wide agency without losing that. Our partnership supported Indigenous-led work in Toronto at a stage when unrestricted funding let the organization build toward its own space and its own programs.

partners.name: Maggie's Toronto Sex Workers Action Project
partners.tagline: Canada's oldest sex-worker justice initiative, offering wrap-around services and life-affirming care across Toronto and the GTA.
partners.serves: Sex workers across Toronto and the GTA
offers: Drop-in and outreach services
Harm reduction supplies and support
Peer-led programming and advocacy
partners.what: Maggie's is run by and for sex workers. It provides harm reduction, drop-in support, outreach, and advocacy grounded in the principle that sex workers are the experts on their own safety and their own lives. It has done this work in Toronto for decades, through changes in law and in public opinion.
partners.why: Maggie's serves a community that most funders avoid, and it does so on its own terms, with leadership drawn from that community. Our partnership reflects a commitment to funding equity-deserving communities where the need is greatest and the funding is scarcest.

partners.name: The Reading Partnership
partners.tagline: Builds literacy programs and resources for families and children in the Kingston-Galloway-Orton Park community of Scarborough.
partners.serves: Children and families in Kingston-Galloway-Orton Park, Scarborough
offers: Parent-led early literacy programs
Reading resources and books for the home
Community events built around reading
partners.what: The Reading Partnership works on the belief that parents are a child's first teachers. In Kingston-Galloway-Orton Park, it trains and supports parents to build reading into daily life, puts books into homes, and runs programs that make literacy a community project rather than a school-only one.
partners.why: The Reading Partnership is community-designed and parent-led, and its results come from a neighbourhood that is often described by its challenges rather than its strengths. Our partnership supports a model that works because the community built it.

partners.name: Toronto Alliance to End Homelessness
partners.tagline: A community-based collective-impact initiative working toward a Toronto where homelessness is rare, brief, and non-recurring.
partners.serves: The homelessness-serving sector in Toronto, and through it, people experiencing homelessness
offers: Coordination across agencies, funders, and government
Data and advocacy for a housing-first system
A platform for people with lived experience to shape policy
partners.what: The Toronto Alliance to End Homelessness brings together the agencies, advocates, and people with lived experience who make up Toronto's homelessness response, and pushes for a system that ends homelessness rather than managing it. Its work is coordination, data, and advocacy, the connective tissue that individual shelters and programs cannot build alone.
partners.why: Systems work is hard to fund because its results show up in other organizations' numbers. Our partnership supports the alliance that makes the whole sector more effective, in keeping with our commitment to systemic equity.

partners.name: Toronto Black Farmers
partners.tagline: A collective of urban farmers and growers building a community food hub focused on food sovereignty, justice, and access to clean food.
partners.serves: Black communities in Toronto seeking access to culturally relevant, clean food
offers: Urban growing sites and a community food hub
Training for new Black farmers and growers
Culturally relevant produce for the community
partners.what: Toronto Black Farmers and Food Growers Collective grows food, trains growers, and builds the infrastructure of a community food hub rooted in Black food traditions. Its work is about sovereignty as much as supply: who owns the land, who grows the food, and who decides what the community eats.
partners.why: Food sovereignty is a long-term project, and a collective of growers cannot plan it on one-year grants. Our partnership supports Black-led work on land, food, and justice in Toronto.

partners.name: Thunder Woman Healing Lodge Society
partners.tagline: Trauma-informed, culturally grounded services and housing for First Nations, Inuit, and Métis 2SLGBTQIA+ women exiting the justice system.
partners.serves: First Nations, Inuit, and Métis women and 2SLGBTQIA+ people leaving the justice system in Toronto
offers: Toronto's first Indigenous women's healing lodge, in development
Culturally grounded, trauma-informed support
Housing and reintegration services
partners.what: Thunder Woman Healing Lodge Society is building Toronto's first healing lodge for Indigenous women and 2SLGBTQIA+ people leaving prison: a place to live, heal, and reconnect with culture rather than a halfway house. Its services are designed by Indigenous women and grounded in ceremony, community, and the understanding that incarceration is one chapter of a longer story.
partners.why: Indigenous women leaving the justice system in Toronto have had nowhere designed for them to go. Our partnership supports an Indigenous-led organization doing work the system has failed to do.

partners.name: Wanasah
partners.tagline: A non-profit mental-health agency addressing the urgent needs of Black youth and their families in Regent Park and surrounding downtown Toronto neighbourhoods.
partners.serves: Black youth and their families in Regent Park and surrounding downtown Toronto neighbourhoods
offers: Counselling and therapy by Black clinicians
Family and community support
Culturally responsive care for Black youth
partners.what: Wanasah provides mental-health care for Black youth and families in Regent Park by clinicians who share their background. It was founded on the recognition that the mainstream system was not reaching Black youth in crisis, and that care has to be culturally responsive, close to home, and free of the barriers that keep families from asking for help.
partners.why: Wanasah is Black-led, neighbourhood-based, and addressing one of the most urgent gaps in Toronto's mental-health system. Our partnership supports an organization built to reach the young people the system was missing.
